title: Data Compression Cuts I/O
description: An uncompressed table reads far more pages than needed for a scan; PAGE compression shrinks it and cuts the I/O. Why it matters: page compression is a low-effort, high-value lever for I/O-bound tables that many teams never enable simply because they don't know the tradeoffs.
narrative:
## Scenario
A 500,000-row `Orders` table is scanned constantly by reports. Many columns are low-cardinality and repetitive (`Status` has 3 values, `Region` is a padded `CHAR(20)` with 4 values). A simple `SELECT COUNT(*)` reads thousands of pages.

## The idea
**Data compression** (`ROW` or `PAGE`) stores more rows per page. `PAGE` compression adds per-page **prefix** and **dictionary** encoding, which is extremely effective on repetitive columns. Fewer pages means every scan and range read performs **fewer logical reads** — a pure I/O win, paid for with a little CPU to decompress.

## What to look for
- Before: a **Clustered Index Scan** reading the full (uncompressed) page count.
- After a `REBUILD ... WITH (DATA_COMPRESSION = PAGE)`: the same scan reads far fewer pages.
- Estimate the savings first with `sys.sp_estimate_data_compression_savings`.

## The fix
`ALTER INDEX PK_Orders ON Orders REBUILD WITH (DATA_COMPRESSION = PAGE);` then re-run the scan. (Compression trades CPU for I/O, so it shines on read-heavy, scan-heavy, compressible tables.)
hints: COUNT(*) scans the clustered index. Its cost is the number of PAGES, not rows -- how could we fit more rows per page?
Region (CHAR(20), 4 values) and Status (3 values) are highly repetitive -- ideal for PAGE dictionary/prefix compression.
ALTER INDEX PK_Orders ON Orders REBUILD WITH (DATA_COMPRESSION = PAGE); then re-run SELECT COUNT(*).
